title: Why Do Wolves Howl? It Is Not About the Moon
summary:
Picture a wolf lifting its head and letting out a long, eerie howl. It is one of the most famous sounds in nature. But wolves are not howling at the moon — that is a myth, says zoologist Arik Kershenbaum of the University of Cambridge. So why do they do it? Experts told Live Science that howling is really about keeping in touch.

Wolves can bark, whimper, yip, squeak and growl, but the howl is their long-distance call. A lone wolf that has become separated from its pack may howl to find its packmates again. When they need to hunt together or care for pups, they need a way to call each other back. A lone wolf that has left its pack may also howl to find a new pack or a mate.

When a whole pack howls together, the chorus can send a message to rival packs: this territory is taken. Data shows that packs howl more in the centre of their territory, when pups are around, and when they have food from a hunt, said Tamás Faragó, an ethologist at Eötvös Loránd University in Budapest. But most group howling is social: it brings the pack together and often happens just before a hunt.

Howling is catching, too. When one wolf hears a howl, it has a very strong tendency to answer back. But a lone wolf that has wandered into a neighbour's territory will stay quiet — answering would give away that it is an intruder. A howl can be heard up to 10 miles (16 kilometres) away in open terrain, according to the Wolf Conservation Center in South Salem, New York. Wolf pups make their first high-pitched attempts at howling when they are between 2 and 4 weeks old.
why_it_matters: Wolves are often misunderstood because of old myths, so learning the real reasons they howl helps people see wild animals more clearly — and shows how scientists test popular beliefs.

background_read: Wolves live and hunt in family groups called packs, and they need ways to talk to each other across long distances.
A howl is a long, loud call that can travel far across open land, much farther than a bark.
Wolves also mark and guard the area where they live and hunt, which they share with their pack.
Scientists who study animal behaviour listen to these calls to learn how wolves stay together, warn rivals, and care for their young.
